explanations.silhouette:
At 16x16 there is room for a shape with more than one idea in it. This apple is a round body with a dip at the top, a stem leaning to the right and a leaf on the left. Block it all in one flat color first.

![Silhouette in one flat color](examples/silhouette.png) ![The finished apple](examples/finished.png)

If the silhouette already reads as an apple, the outline and shading only have to confirm it.
explanations.outline:
A curve in pixels is a staircase. Read each edge as runs: straight pieces of 1, 2, 3 or more pixels. A clean curve keeps its runs steady, or lets them grow or shrink one step at a time as the curve turns.

![Clean outline](examples/outline.png) ![A jaggy on the right side](examples/jaggy.png) ![A double on the bottom left](examples/doubles.png)

The middle apple has a **jaggy**: one pixel on the right side sticks out, breaking a straight run of 4 into pieces. The last one has a **double**: an extra pixel in the corner of a diagonal step, which makes the line look thick there. Keep the line 1 pixel wide and let diagonal pixels touch only at their corners.
explanations.base:
Two materials, two base colors: red for the apple and teal for the leaf. The red is already down from the silhouette, so add the leaf inside its outline.

![Outline and base colors](examples/flat.png)
explanations.shadow:
The light comes from the top right, so the shadow wraps round the bottom left: a band 1 to 2 pixels wide inside the outline, thickest at the bottom.

The shadow is not a darker red. It shifts toward purple, the same family as the outline, which keeps the palette small and makes the shadow feel cool.

![Flat](examples/flat.png) ![With shadow](examples/shaded.png)
explanations.highlight:
A small white cross on the upper right is where the light hits hardest. Five pixels are enough. A highlight is the brightest color on the sprite, and it only works if there is very little of it.

![With shadow](examples/shaded.png) ![With the highlight](examples/finished.png)
